newsitem.title: USA: CMS CEO sees no federal retail wheeling law.
newsitem.headline: CMS CEO sees no federal retail wheeling law.

text.p: There will be significant changes in the electric power industry over the next few years, but they will not include federal legislation mandating retail electric wheeling, CMS Energy Corp chief executive William T. McCormick Jr told Reuters.

Elaborating on his speech to the Aurthur Andersen 17th Annual Energy Symposium in Houston, he said Congress will not act due to substantial opposition and progress by individual states addressing electric restructuring issues.
Stating the proposals are "too controversial," he said there is "not enough support to get (them) out of committee."

McCormick cited organized opposition to Federal retail wheeling legislation from utilities, environmental groups, the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners and many legislators who favor state purview over retail utility restructuring issues.

"Because several states have already approved retail access plans and a number of others are considering them, Federal legislation will likely be overtaken" by the implementation of state plans, he told the symposium.
By the end of 1997, McCormick explained in a telephone interview, enough states will have acted so "people will look at this and say 'we don't need'" federal legislation.

He told the symposium there probably will be opportunities for repeal of the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, which regulates U.S. utilities, and address several other specific utility regulatory issues, such as amending the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 and removing subsidies to public power entities.
McCormick forecast significant changes in the electric utility industry, including:
* Universal access to alternative electric supplies at the wholesale level within one year;
* Limited state-authorized retail wheeling in the near term with increasingly prevalent negotiated discount power supply agreements between utilities and large industrial and wholesale customers;
* Movement toward providing total energy management to larger customers rather than sales of specific fuels; and
* A continued wave of utility mergers to form fewer, larger utilities and acquisition by larger energy companies of most independent power companies.
Within five years, McCormick said, he expects companies remaining in the industry to "settle" into one of five catagories.
-- Medium-to-large multicompany domestic integrated utilities that will result because companies "perceive the need to achieve economies of scale to reduce unit costs and become more compettitive.
"While these companies become bigger through the mergers, their growth rates are limited largely to the growth of their combined service areas," he pointed out.
The second category is small-to-medium sized one-state distribution utilities that purchase most of their power.
McCormick said he expects "some states may attempt" to force creation of this type of company by divestment of generation assets, adding this "will not be that wide spread."

The third category includes large merged natural gas and elctric companies such as the ones that Duke Power Co and PanEnergy Corp, and Houston Industries Inc and NorAm Energy Corp are seeking to form.

"The fourth category is what I call the international energy companies ... that are taking advantage of the opportunities in other countries for investement in power plants and other energy infrastructure.
He said these "companies are embarked on growth strategies because the energy demand growth rates in these countries are twice or even three times the 2.5-to-3 percent or so in the United States."

And, finally, "there will be a continued shakeout in the independent power industries with the smaller to medium-sized companies being acquired by the larger, mostly utility-affiliated major companies, with only a few large, independent power generators surviving."
McCormick said CMS will be one of the international energy companies.

He said "we intend to keep our generation," noting Michigan regulators do not seem interested in divestment; adding CMS has "no plans to merge our (regulated distribution) utility." -- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.
